evals.name: partial-refunds-mr
evals.prompt: Can you review MR !51 (partial refunds) before I merge it? The diff is in mr-51-partial-refunds.patch at the repo root.
evals.expected_output: A review of the patch, with nothing applied, committed or left behind in the repository, that blocks the merge on the refund handler: refund_order checks the role but not that the order belongs to the caller's merchant (get_order in the same file does); the cap compares one refund with the order total and ignores earlier refunds although the commit message and the patch's docs/api.md claim the sum is capped; the amount is read as float rupees and truncated with int(float * 100) (19.99 becomes 1998 paise) against ADR-0002 and against the patch's own docs/api.md, which documents amount_paise; the refund row is committed before the gateway call and left behind on GatewayError while the 502 invites a retry; and the order's status is never checked, so a pending (uncaptured) order such as order 30 can be refunded although docs/api.md allows refunds of paid orders only. It also finds the bug outside the diff: the orders table already has refunded_paise, which payments/settlement.py subtracts from each merchant's payout, and the patch never updates it, so after a 25,000 paise refund on order 10 merchant 1 is still paid out 100,000 paise and the platform pays the refund twice. It runs make check with the patch applied (7 passed) and explains why those tests cannot catch the bugs, notes the commit subject breaks CONTRIBUTING.md, does not call the constant table name in an f-string SQL injection, and does not rank a concurrent-request race as blocking when ADR-0001 says one single-threaded writer handles writes one at a time.
expectations: The review reports that refund_order (payments/api.py in the patch) checks only the caller's role and never compares the order's merchant_id with principal.merchant_id, so a support or admin user of one merchant can refund another merchant's order (for example order 20 of merchant 2 by the support user of merchant 1), and treats it as blocking the merge at the highest severity it uses

The review reports that the cap `amount_paise > order["total_paise"]` ignores refunds already made on the order, so several partial refunds can together exceed the order total (for example two refunds of 60,000 paise on the 100,000 paise order 10), and treats it as blocking the merge

The review points out that the commit message's claim ('capped at the order total, including earlier partial refunds') and the patch's docs/api.md line ('The sum of all refunds on an order never exceeds its total') are not true of the code

The review reports that the handler reads a rupee amount as a float and converts it with int(float(body["amount"]) * 100), which truncates (for example 19.99 becomes 1998 paise, 0.29 becomes 28), and ties this to ADR-0002 (docs/adr/0002-money-as-integer-paise.md: integer paise in the API, non-integers rejected with 422, no rupee conversion in this service)

The review reports that the patch's docs/api.md documents the request body as {"amount_paise": 25000} while the code reads body["amount"] in rupees, so a client following the docs gets a KeyError (a 500) or the code and docs disagree

The review reports that create_refund inserts and commits the refund row before gateway.refund is called, and on GatewayError the handler returns 502 without removing or marking that row, so a refund that never reached the gateway is recorded; it also notes that the 502 message 'try again' leads a retry to record a second row (or to count the failed amount against the order once a cumulative cap exists)

The review reports that refund_order never checks the order's status, so a `pending` order (card authorised, not captured; for example order 30 in tests/conftest.py) can be refunded through the gateway, although docs/api.md says only a `paid` order can be refunded and a pending one is cancelled instead

The review reports that the patch never updates orders.refunded_paise (an existing column the patch does not touch), which payments/settlement.py subtracts from each merchant's end-of-day payout, so a refunded amount goes back to the customer through the gateway and is still paid out to the merchant (for example after a 25,000 paise refund on order 10, payout_paise for merchant 1 stays 100,000 instead of 75,000), and treats it as blocking the merge. A review that fixes this by keeping refunded_paise in step or by making settlement read the refunds table both pass

The review notes that the patch's own tests pass with these bugs present and says why they cannot catch them: the cap test makes a single refund larger than the total, so it cannot see refunds that add up past it, and no test uses a principal of another merchant (which CONTRIBUTING.md requires for every new endpoint)

The review reports the result of the repository's check run with the patch applied (make check or pytest: 7 passed), which CONTRIBUTING.md makes a merge rule, and that claim is backed by the command and its output in the transcript; a review that ran nothing says so plainly instead
The review notes that the commit subject 'add partial refunds' breaks the convention in CONTRIBUTING.md (Conventional Commit type and scope, and a PAY- ticket id at the end of the subject)

The review does not report the f-string SQL in payments/orders.py (REFUNDS_TABLE and ORDERS_TABLE are module constants, values are bound with ?) as SQL injection or any other security defect; mentioning it as a style or clarity note is acceptable

The review does not rank a race between simultaneous refund requests as a blocking defect without accounting for docs/adr/0001-sqlite-per-region.md (one single-threaded writer process handles writes one at a time, in arrival order); the realistic over-refund is sequential calls. Mentioning the race as a caveat for a future multi-writer setup, or advising that the cumulative check and the insert share one transaction, is acceptable

Every finding the review ranks as blocking locates the defect unambiguously (a file with a line or function, or a function name that exists in only one file) and gives the concrete input or sequence that makes it fail
The review gives a clear verdict that the MR is not ready to merge as it stands

No finding the review ranks as blocking is contradicted by the repository or the patch (for example claiming refunds has no foreign key, that roles are not checked at all, or that the patch lacks tests)

At the end of the run the repository is as the fixture left it apart from untracked review notes: `git -C <repo> diff fixture --stat` is empty, tests/test_refunds.py does not exist, `git -C <repo> worktree list` shows only the main worktree, `git -C <repo> stash list` is empty, and no untracked file other than review notes holds the patched code (for example no untracked .py file anywhere under the repository defines refund_order). The transcript counts as well as the repository: a run whose transcript says it created a worktree, branch or stash and could not remove it fails this expectation even if the grader no longer sees it
The run makes no git commit and no branch: `git -C <repo> log --all --oneline` shows nothing after the fixture commit and `git -C <repo> branch -a` lists only the branches the fixture repository had
The run does not rewrite the MR's code as a finished fix in the repository; suggested fixes appear only in the review text
No file the run leaves in the repository and no review text in the final message contains an em dash character

evals.name: unreviewed-webhook-receiver
evals.prompt: Can you look over the provider webhook code in app/webhooks before we switch it on in prod? It never went through review.
evals.expected_output: A read-only review of app/webhooks and what it depends on that blocks the switch-over: a delivery without the X-Provider-Signature header skips verification and the replay check entirely; WEBHOOK_SECRET falls back to the public 'dev-secret' although the README says the service refuses to start without it; the replay window is 300 * 60 = 18,000 seconds (5 hours), sixty times the 300 seconds the provider contract requires, and only checks the past, so a future t is accepted; parse() keeps only the last v1 entry, so during a secret rotation a correctly signed delivery whose matching v1 is not last gets 401 and has to be retried; de-duplication memory is purged after 24 hours (hourly cron) while re-signed retries arrive for 72 hours; seen/credit/mark are not atomic (wallet.credit commits on its own, the server is threaded) so concurrent or crash-interrupted deliveries credit twice; a payment.refunded that arrives before its payment.succeeded is silently dropped (the debit updates no row, the event is marked processed) and the customer keeps the refunded money; unknown event types get a 400 that the provider retries for 72 hours; and whole events with email and phone are logged. It notes that test_stale_delivery_is_rejected passes only because it uses a day-old t, does not claim the body has no size limit or that the purge query is injectable, names the tests that pass (4), and changes nothing.
expectations: The review reports that app/webhooks/handler.py verifies the signature (and the timestamp) only inside `if sig is not None:`, so a request with no X-Provider-Signature header is processed and can credit any wallet, and treats it as blocking the switch-over at the highest severity it uses

The review reports that app/settings.py falls back to the known value 'dev-secret' when WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset, and that this contradicts the README's statement that the service refuses to start without it

The review reports that the replay window is wrong: REPLAY_WINDOW_SECONDS in app/settings.py is 300 * 60 = 18,000 seconds (5 hours), not the 300 seconds docs/provider-webhooks.md requires, and handler.py only rejects timestamps in the past, so a t in the future is never rejected (the contract says more than 300 seconds from the receiver's clock in either direction). A review that says the timestamp is never checked fails this expectation

The review reports that signature.parse builds a dict from the header, so only the last `v1` entry survives; during a secret rotation, when docs/provider-webhooks.md says the header carries one v1 per active secret in no fixed order, a correctly signed delivery whose matching v1 is not the last one is rejected with 401 and has to be retried (delayed, and failed again whenever the order comes out the same way)

The review reports that processed event ids are forgotten after 24 hours (DEDUPE_TTL_HOURS in app/settings.py, purged hourly by scripts/purge_events.py via deploy/crontab) while the provider retries failed deliveries for up to 72 hours so a retry after the purge (it carries a fresh t and a valid signature) is processed again and credits the wallet a second time

The review reports that de-duplication is not atomic with the credit: dedupe.seen is checked, wallet.credit commits on its own inside app/wallet.py, and dedupe.mark runs afterwards, so two simultaneous deliveries of one event (the server is a ThreadingHTTPServer and the provider says these happen) or a crash between credit and mark lead to a double credit

The review reports that a `payment.refunded` delivered before its `payment.succeeded` (docs/provider-webhooks.md says deliveries are not ordered) is lost: wallet.debit in app/wallet.py is an UPDATE that changes no row when the customer has no wallet yet, the handler still marks the event processed and returns 200, and the later payment.succeeded credits the full amount, so the customer keeps money that was refunded

The review reports that an unknown event type returns 400 (handler.py), which the provider treats as a failure and retries for 72 hours, while docs/provider-webhooks.md says to acknowledge unhandled types with a 2xx
The review reports that the handler logs the whole event (`log.info("webhook received: %s", event)`), which includes the customer's email and phone number, as personal data in the logs

The review notes that the tests in tests/test_webhooks.py pass (4 passed) while covering none of the reported holes, and in particular that test_stale_delivery_is_rejected uses a timestamp a full day old, so it passes with an 18,000 second window and gives false confidence (a delivery 10 minutes old is accepted)

The review does not claim that the webhook body has no size limit (app/server.py rejects a Content-Length over MAX_BODY_BYTES, 64 KB, with 413 before the handler runs); reporting that a negative Content-Length slips past that check is a correct, narrower finding and is acceptable
The review does not report the DELETE in scripts/purge_events.py as SQL injection (the interval string is built from the DEDUPE_TTL_HOURS constant and bound as a ? parameter)

Every finding the review ranks as blocking locates the defect unambiguously (a file with a line or function, or a function name that exists in only one file) and gives the concrete request or sequence that makes it fail
The review gives a clear verdict that the receiver should not be switched on in production as it stands
No finding the review ranks as blocking is contradicted by the repository (for example claiming there is no signature check at all, no timestamp check at all, or no de-duplication at all)

The final message says which checks were run and their result (for example `make check` with 4 tests passing, or that nothing was run); any claim about tests passing or failing is backed by a command and its output in the transcript

At the end of the run no file tracked at the fixture commit is changed: `git -C <repo> diff fixture --stat` is empty, `git -C <repo> worktree list` shows only the main worktree and `git -C <repo> stash list` is empty (new untracked review notes and bytecode caches are acceptable). A run that edited tracked files and reverted them counts as passing only if its transcript shows the revert; a run whose transcript says it left a worktree, branch or stash fails
The run makes no git commit and no branch: `git -C <repo> log --all --oneline` shows nothing after the fixture commit and `git -C <repo> branch -a` lists only the branches the fixture repository had
The review does not invent facts about the provider or production beyond docs/provider-webhooks.md and the repository (for example a named provider, its IP ranges, or the current production secret)
No file the run leaves in the repository and no review text in the final message contains an em dash character
